agent_7.question: Which existing institutional mechanism (e.g., the community leader, a vote, or another role) is intended to hold the authority to impose the one‑week fishing ban, and how will that authority be exercised?
agent_7.answer: The community leader is the authority to impose the one‑week fishing ban. The leader reviews the shared ledger each week, checks if a fisher’s cumulative catch exceeds the 2 kg per‑trip or 6 kg per‑week limits or pushes the community total beyond 30 % of stock, and then formally issues a one‑week ban on the offending fisher(s), requiring them to return any excess catch.

agent_7.question: Who receives the fish that a fisher must return after a ban, and how is the return process carried out?
agent_7.answer: The fish that a fisher must give back go straight into the community’s common pool. The leader takes them in, notes the amount in the ledger, and keeps them on a shared shelf. When the next fishing week starts, those fish can be re‑issued to anyone who still needs a catch or can be used for communal purposes, like feeding the school or selling to a nearby market. The key point is that no one keeps the excess; it stays with the community and is made available to those who need it.

agent_7.question: When and by whom is the lake’s current stock measured each week, and how is that measurement recorded and used to compare to the 30 % threshold?
agent_7.answer: In our lake we treat the stock as a shared resource, so the community leader (or the person appointed as the observer for the week) takes the measurement at the start of each week, just after the night and before anyone goes out to fish. agent_7.question: How does the community decide who receives the returned fish in the communal pool, and what procedure is followed to redistribute those fish in future weeks?

The ledger notes who got what, and the leader can rotate the order each week if some fishers are always the first to receive shares. This keeps the process transparent and fair, so no one feels short‑changed.

agent_8.question: When is the monthly steward elected, by what procedure, and what happens if no majority vote is achieved?
agent_8.answer:
In our small lake community we treat the steward as the person who keeps the ledger straight and makes sure the rules are followed.  We elect the steward on the first fishing day of each month – usually the first Wednesday that we all head out together – by a secret ballot among all fishers.  A simple majority (more than half of the votes cast) is required.  If no one gets a majority – for example a perfect tie – we hold a runoff election the following day with only the candidates who tied.  If the runoff also fails to produce a majority (rare, but possible if we’re short on people), the current steward keeps the job until the next scheduled monthly election, so the ledger stays under someone’s watch and we don’t lose any fishers’ catches to administrative chaos.

That’s the process that keeps us all honest and makes sure the communal pool is handled fairly.

agent_8.question: If a fisher’s reserve is below 12 kg and they catch less than 5 kg, how can they keep 4 kg and still contribute an additional 1 kg to the pool? What happens in that case?
agent_8.answer:
If my reserve is under 12 kg and I only catch 4.3 kg, I can’t keep the usual 4 kg and still put an extra 1 kg into the pool, because I simply don’t have enough fish to do both. In that situation I have to deposit the entire 4.3 kg into the pool and keep nothing for that trip. The 1‑kg contribution rule takes precedence over the 4‑kg keep rule when my reserve is low – it’s a way of keeping the lake’s fish supply fair for everyone.

So, if you catch less than 5 kg while below 12 kg, you log the total catch, deposit the whole catch into the pool, and keep 0 kg. If you catch 5 kg or more, you keep 4 kg, deposit the remainder, and also set aside an extra 1 kg from that remainder to add to the pool (so the amount deposited equals catch‑4 kg + 1 kg).

The suspension is announced on the community notice board, posted to the community chat, and the monitor sends a direct message to every fisher reminding them that fishing is forbidden until the stock rises to at least the 25 % reserve level.  The monitor also records the suspension in the official log and ensures that any fisher who attempts to fish during the ban is required to perform community service and return the fish to the reserve.  When the monitor later records that the stock has recovered to 25 % or more of last month’s stock, the ban is lifted and a new notice is posted.

This process keeps the decision transparent, accountable, and tied to the measured stock, ensuring that the community can act quickly to protect the lake’s long‑term sustainability.

agent_2.question: What method or instrument does the monitor use to record the lake’s current stock at the start of each month?

The catch from the net is weighed on a calibrated digital scale to obtain a sample biomass. By knowing the volume of water sampled (net area × average depth at that point) the monitor extrapolates to an estimate of the total lake stock for that month. This simple, repeatable method keeps the estimate accurate enough for our community rules while requiring only a net and a scale, which we already have on the boat.

agent_2.question: How does the community ensure the reserve remains at least 25% of the lake’s stock, and who monitors and enforces that reserve level?
agent_2.answer:

If any fisher ends up taking more than 0.5 kg on a single trip, the excess must be deposited in the communal reserve tank and noted in the log – that keeps the reserve from dipping below 25 %. If the FOG finds that the reserve is projected to fall below 25 %, the community will suspend fishing for 30 days or until the reserve is back above the threshold, whichever comes first. This way everyone knows who is watching, how the reserve is measured, and how the rules are kept.

The community will monitor and enforce the reserve level through the FOG’s monthly surveys and log audits, and by requiring any excess fish be returned to the reserve tank. The FOG also handles disputes and issues a communal warning or temporary suspension for repeated violations.

That’s the plan – it keeps the lake healthy and our future secure.

agent_4.answer: The person who estimates the lake biomass and sets the monthly community cap is the Community Fishery Committee, which is made up of fishers who serve in a rotating leadership role each month. The inspector’s decisions are recorded publicly and can be reviewed by the committee if a fisher contests a suspension.  This system keeps the inspector independent of the fishing effort, ensures impartial enforcement, and maintains community trust.

agent_5.question: What is the fish council, and who makes up its membership and authority to enforce the rule?
agent_5.answer: The fish council is the community’s own governing body, elected each month by a simple majority of the active fishers.  It consists of the ten fisher representatives who sit on the lake ledger board, plus a rotating steward chosen by the council to keep records.  The council’s authority comes from the collective consent we’ve built through voting on rules—when a rule passes with a majority, the council is empowered to enforce it.  It can levy fines, confiscate excess fish, or deny future permits until the violation is cured.

agent_5.question: What is the procedure the council follows when a fisher breaches the 50% monthly cap—specifically how it determines whether to forfeit excess fish or impose a fine, and what those actions entail?
agent_5.answer:
When a fisher’s monthly haul goes past the 50 % cap, the council first pulls the ledger for that month and computes the excess (the amount by which the fisher’s cumulative take exceeds half the lake’s stock at the month’s start). The council then contacts the fisher.  If the fisher brings back the excess fish before the next council meeting, the council records the return and clears any penalty – the fisher keeps the rest of their haul.  If the excess is not returned, the council has two options:
1. **Forfeit the excess** – the fisher is required to deposit the excess kg into the community pool (the communal reserve that is used to help those who run low or to fund shared maintenance).  This is a hard penalty that removes the fish from the fisher’s personal stock.
2. **Impose a fine** – the council levies a fine equal to 5 % of the market value of the excess kg, or if that is impractical, a flat $1 per kg of excess.  The fine is paid into the community’s shared fund.  The council prefers forfeiture for first‑time offenders; repeated breaches trigger fines.
The decision is recorded in the ledger, and the fisher’s name is flagged for the next monthly review.  This keeps the rule enforceable, transparent, and fair to everyone.

This procedure doesn’t change my proposal – it just clarifies how the council would act when the rule is broken.

agent_5.question: What criteria does the council use to decide whether to forfeit excess fish or impose a fine for a breach?
agent_5.answer: Council decides based on four factors. Fourth, if the excess exceeds 1 kg or if the fisher has a history of repeated breaches, the council will forfeit the excess fish to the community pool, or, if the fisher insists on keeping it, they will be fined the same 5 % of market value or $1 per kg but also have to pay a mandatory community fund contribution of $1 per kg of the excess. The council also reviews the fisher’s intent: an accidental over‑take is treated more leniently than a deliberate over‑take. In short, voluntary return = no penalty; small unreturned excess = warning/fine; large or repeated excess = forfeit or heavy fine plus fund contribution.

The council also looks for evidence such as a fisher deliberately rounding down the reported lake stock or ignoring the trip report. In short, intentional breaches are judged by repeated or purposeful violations and evidence of deceit; accidental breaches are judged by a clean prior record and reasonable errors.

agent_5.answer: The council uses two main factors: the size of the excess and the fisher’s recent compliance history. If the excess is 4 kg or more, or if the fisher has had more than one breach in the past three months, the council will forfeit the extra fish to the community pool. For smaller excesses and for fishers with a clean record, the council will impose a fine of 5 % of the excess fish’s market value (or $1 per kg, whichever is higher).
agent_5.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 25% of the lake’s current stock per trip, capped at 8 kg, and may not cumulatively take more than 50% of the lake’s stock at the start of each calendar month.
agent_5.revised_operationalization: Before each trip, a fisher records the lake’s current stock from the community ledger and calculates 25% of that amount. If the calculation exceeds 8 kg, the fisher may only take 8 kg that trip. After the trip, the fisher submits a trip report to the fish council. The council tracks monthly totals for each fisher and flags any who would exceed the 50 % monthly cap. If a fisher breaches the cap, the council first asks for voluntary return of the excess. If the excess is not returned, the council calculates the excess amount, checks the fisher’s compliance history and the size of the excess, and then either forfeit the excess fish to the community pool or impose a fine of 5 % of the excess fish’s market value (or $1 per kg) into the shared fund, depending on the criteria above.

agent_6.question: Who is responsible for maintaining and updating the shared ledger that records the reserve bin holdings?
agent_6.answer: As the ledger is community‑held, each fisher is responsible for recording his or her haul and the reserve amount before departing. If a fisher forgets or misreports, the community may correct the ledger and seize the missing 4 kg. We can appoint a rotating keeper (for example the fisher with the longest tenure that round) to double‑check entries, but the ultimate duty remains with each fisher.
agent_6.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 40 kg per trip, but the lake must always retain a minimum reserve of 20 kg; if the reserve falls below 20 kg, each fisher must set aside 4 kg of their catch before leaving.
agent_6.revised_operationalization: Before departing, a fisher tallies their haul and calculates the lake’s post‑trip reserve. If the reserve is under 20 kg, the fisher is required to drop 4 kg into a community‑held reserve bin on the dock. All reserves are logged on a shared ledger visible to everyone. If a fisher fails to set aside the required 4 kg when the reserve is low, the community may immediately seize that portion of the fisher’s haul and reduce that fisher’s future quota. The reserve bin is replenished only by new catch, ensuring the 20 kg floor is maintained.

agent_6.question: What is the process for determining a fisher's future quota and how is that quota reduced if a fisher fails to set aside the required 4 kg?
agent_6.answer: If I don't drop the 4 kg when the lake’s below 20 kg, the dock crew will grab it from my boat right there. They'll write it on the ledger and then, when we next meet, they'll cut my next‑trip quota by the same amount I didn’t set aside – usually 4 kg or a bit more if I’ve done it before. The idea is that the fewer kilos I put in the bin, the smaller my allowance becomes, so I’ll have to stay below the 40 kg limit on future trips until I’ve caught enough to rebuild the reserve.

agent_6.question: What determines the proportionally larger penalty for a fisher who repeats a violation of failing to set aside the required 4 kg?
agent_6.answer: The larger penalty is driven by how many times you’ve slipped on the set‑aside rule. For each repeat the crew will raise the seizure and the quota cut in a fixed step: first slip, 4 kg seized; second slip, 8 kg seized and your next‑trip quota lowered by 8 kg; third slip, 12 kg seized and quota cut by 12 kg, and so on. The idea is to keep the penalty proportional to the number of past failures so that repeat offenders are pushed to keep the reserve steady.

agent_6.question: Under what conditions and by whom is a fisher’s next‑trip quota restored to the standard limit after they have complied with the reserve rule?
agent_6.answer: In our little lake, the rule on hand says that a penalty – the seizure and a drop in next‑trip quota – is only applied after a fisher breaks the reserve rule. There is no separate penalty schedule that keeps a fisher on a reduced quota; the quota reverts as soon as compliance is proven and the community agrees to restore it.

agent_7.answer: The pot is held by the Fishery Council, with the rotating observer acting as its custodian during their shift. All surplus deposits go into the pot, and the Council disburses it for restoration projects when the lake’s stock falls below 5kg.

Surplus from any trip that exceeds 1kg must be deposited into a community pot that is held by the Fishery Council and used to restore the lake when stocks dip below 5kg.

agent_7.question: How is surplus fish from trips that exceed 1 kg turned into monetary funds in the community pot, and what is the process for depositing those funds?
agent_7.answer: Hey folks, when I haul in a bit more than the 1 kg that’s allowed per trip, the extra fish (the surplus) doesn’t just sit on the boat. We sell the surplus at that price, get the cash, and then the council’s treasurer puts the money into the community pot’s bank account. That whole thing happens the same day or within 24 hours. The council keeps a ledger entry for the sale, updates the pot balance, and reports it in the monthly update. That way the lake’s excess catch gets turned into real money that can be used for restoration when we need it. This is the process we follow so the policy stays clear and everyone knows how the funds come in.

agent_8.question: The proposal refers to each fisher’s reserve, but the current state doesn’t track a reserve—how is a fisher’s reserve defined or tracked?
agent_8.answer: My reserve is the weight of fish I have gathered and kept in my boat’s storage or at home. After each trip I add the catch I keep (between 1–5 kg) to my reserve, subtract any that I’ve eaten or sold, and record the net in my personal ledger. The community ledger has a column for each fisher’s reserve, updated every trip, so the council can see who’s under 15 kg or 10 kg when it’s time to split the pool or enforce the extra‑contribution rule.

All transactions are recorded in the community ledger and repeated violations lead to a temporary fishing ban.

agent_8.answer: The ban is a community decision, not a unilateral power. Whenever a fisher has three violations in the same month, the community council – the group of fishers who sign the monthly agreement – will record a temporary ban on the ledger. That ban lasts for two fishing trips (roughly a week). If the fisher breaks the rule again after the ban, the council can extend the ban by another two trips. All of this is noted in the ledger so everyone knows who’s banned and for how long.

Once the month ends the council does a review; if you haven’t hit three violations the counter simply goes back to zero and the ban field is cleared. agent_9.question: Who constitutes the community council, and how is it established and its authority determined?
agent_9.answer: The council is simply the elected voice of the fishing community. Each of us—every family or individual who spends a day on the lake—has one vote in a simple secret ballot held at the beginning of each month. The candidates are any fishers who volunteer, and the top three (or five, if we want a broader view) get chosen as council members. They sit together each day after we finish our trips, compare the tally sheet and the lake’s current biomass, and enforce the limits. The council’s authority comes from the community charter that we all signed after round 11, which says that any rule adopted by the council must be followed by all fishers. If a fisher violates a rule, the council can order a donation to the reserve fund or, for repeated offenders, a one‑day ban, as we’ve all agreed. The council’s decisions are binding because they’re backed by that charter and by the mutual need to keep the lake alive.

The council sums the intended catches and compares them to 25 % of the current lake biomass; if the total would exceed the limit, each fisher must proportionally reduce their catch until the limit is met. The council records actual catches after each trip. If a fisher exceeds the 1 kg per trip rule or the daily community limit, the fisher is required to donate an equivalent amount of their catch to the community reserve fund. Violations are tracked, and repeated offenders face a temporary fishing ban of one day.

agent_9.question: Where is the community reserve fund recorded, and how is it tracked and used within the community state?
agent_9.answer:
The reserve fund is kept in the communal chest that the council guards at the village hall. Every day after the tally sheet is tallied, any fish that must be donated is moved from the fisher’s catch to the chest. The council then records the amount in the community ledger, a simple log that lists the date, the amount donated, and the person who donated it. The ledger is kept in the council’s office and is posted on the community notice board, so every fisher can see how much the reserve holds at any time.

The reserve is used only for the good of the whole community. The council can decide to use it to pay for repairs to nets and boats, to provide food during lean months, or to buy supplies for the fish‑catching infrastructure. No one can withdraw from the reserve for personal use; any such withdrawal must be recorded in the ledger and approved by the council.

This system keeps the reserve visible and accountable, and it discourages fishing beyond the limits because the penalty is a direct loss of the fisher’s catch into the communal pot.

agent_9.question: How and when does the council measure and record the lake’s current biomass to determine the 25 % daily removal limit?
agent_9.answer: We measure the lake’s biomass at the start of every fishing day, right before anyone submits his intended catch. A council volunteer teams up with a handful of fishers to perform a quick standard net sweep along the shoreline, catches a representative sample, weighs it, and then applies the community’s established multiplier (catch weight ÷ sample volume × lake surface area) to estimate the total biomass. That estimate is logged in the council ledger, and the 25 % daily removal limit is calculated from it. Because the measurement is done first thing in the morning, everyone knows the limit before the day’s work begins and can adjust their intended catches accordingly. The ledger records the estimate so we can see how the limit has changed from day to day.

agent_4.question: The proposal does not specify who holds the community monitor role or how that person is selected or appointed.
agent_4.answer:
I think the monitor should be someone the whole community trusts, not someone who gets to fish and also check the ledger. We could have each fisher be eligible to serve as monitor, but we’d rotate the duty so no one keeps it for long. The simplest way is to hold a short community meeting at the start of each month and let everyone vote for who will be the monitor for that month. A simple majority wins; if there’s a tie, we draw lots from the names of the voters. That way, the role stays open and transparent, and no single person can abuse it. If for some reason a fisher refuses or cannot serve, we’ll open the vote again until someone accepts. This keeps the process fair and the monitoring impartial.

The community monitor calculates total removal over the last 30 days; if it exceeds 10 % of current biomass, all fishing is halted for 7 days. Biomass is measured quarterly via community sampling; if below 3 kg, all fishing stops until measured biomass reaches 6 kg, then a 30‑day rest period before fishing resumes.

Monitor selection: Every month, during a short community meeting, all fishers vote for who will act as the monitor for that month. Anyone eligible can run. This way the monitoring remains impartial, transparent, and shared among us.

agent_4.question: The proposal does not specify how the community knows when the lake’s biomass has fallen below 3 kg or risen to 6 kg to trigger the fishing suspension and rest period, particularly between the quarterly sampling events.
agent_4.answer: We can keep a running estimate of the lake’s biomass between the quarterly samplings by using the catch logs we all already keep. Every week the community monitor will add up the total weight removed in the past 30 days from the ledger, add a simple growth estimate (for example, a 5 % increase per week based on our known reproduction rate), and subtract that from the last measured biomass. That gives us an approximate current biomass. If that estimate drops below 3 kg, the monitor will announce a suspension of all fishing until the estimate rises above 6 kg; once it does, we still observe a 30‑day rest before fishing resumes. To validate the estimate, the monitor will also do a quick 5‑m² net sampling once a month and record that result in the ledger.

I think it’s fair to have a clear path for repeat offenders.  Each violation is noted on the ledger and the fisher receives a formal warning.  If the same fisher violates again within the next 30 days, the community forms a small enforcement committee of respected fishers who will suspend that fisher’s license for 30 days. agent_5.question: How is a fisher’s obligation to return excess weight to the lake after exceeding the monthly limit enforced, and who verifies that it has been done?
agent_5.answer: In the way we run it, the log keeper is the official recorder and the community is the watchdog. Every trip the fisherman puts his catch on the log and the log keeper notes the weight and the current lake stock. At the start of the month the log keeper tells everyone what the 70 % monthly limit is. If a fisherman ends up taking more than that limit, the log keeper and the other fishers immediately see that the total on the log exceeds the limit. The rule is that the fisherman must put the extra kilos back in the lake right away and must not keep any more catch for the rest of the month. The log keeper writes that return in the log, and the rest of the crew checks that the lake’s stock has increased accordingly. If a fisherman refuses to return the excess, the crew can call a quick meeting, and if the consensus is that he violated the rule, we impose a penalty as we decided in a past vote. So the enforcement is a combination of the log keeper’s official record and the crew’s collective oversight – nobody gets to cheat the system because everyone can see the numbers and can ask the fisherman to correct it.

agent_6.question: Who holds the 4 kg deposit that each fisher must put into the reserve, and how is that deposit recorded on the shared ledger?
agent_6.answer: The 4 kg deposit is kept in the lake’s reserve by the steward. After each fisher logs their total catch, they record a separate line item for the 4 kg set‑aside that is transferred from them to the reserve. The ledger shows the fisher’s name, the amount caught, the 4 kg deposit, and the updated reserve total. If a fisher fails to make the deposit, the steward adds the missing 4 kg to the reserve and records it as a forfeited amount, then charges the fisher an extra 1 kg penalty that goes to the community pool.

agent_6.question: Does the 4 kg deposit count toward the 35 kg per‑trip limit, or is it an additional amount the fisher can take?
agent_6.answer:
The 4 kg deposit is not part of what you keep – it’s a contribution that must be taken out of your catch before you can claim the rest. In other words, the 35 kg per‑trip limit applies to the total amount you bring in, but the 4 kg you must set aside (if the reserve is too low) is deducted from that amount and goes straight into the reserve. So if you catch 35 kg when the reserve falls below 18 kg, you can only keep 31 kg; the 4 kg goes to the reserve. If the reserve is fine, you can keep all 35 kg and set aside nothing.

agent_7.question: Who is the rotating chair that reviews logs, and how is the chair rotation determined?
agent_7.answer: The rotating chair is the fisher who is selected each week by a simple lottery among all fishers who are not currently fishing. The chair changes every week, ensuring every fisher eventually takes the role. The lottery is drawn at the start of the week, and the fishers who are fishing that week are excluded from the draw to avoid conflicts of interest.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 2 kg per trip, and the total weekly harvest must not exceed 40% of the current lake stock, with a hard minimum of 3 kg remaining in the lake.

If a fisher exceeds the 2 kg per trip limit or the total harvest exceeds the 40% threshold, the excess fish must be returned within 24 hours and the fisher must attend a community meeting. Repeat violations result in a temporary fishing ban.

agent_7.question: How is the lake’s stock measured each week, and who performs the measurement?
agent_7.answer: We measure the lake’s stock each week by taking a sample net catch from a fixed spot at the start of the week and weighing it. The rotating chair—chosen by lottery among fishers who aren’t fishing that week—does the catch, records the weight, and uses a simple scaling factor to estimate the total stock of the lake. Two other fishers present at the time verify the weight and confirm the estimate before it is entered into the shared ledger. That measurement is the basis for calculating the 40 % weekly limit and the 3 kg minimum that must remain in the lake.

agent_7.question: How is the simple scaling factor used to estimate the total lake stock determined and agreed upon?
agent_7.answer:
The scaling factor is decided by a simple math that all of us can see. The rotating chair picks a sample net in a spot that we agree is representative of the lake, weighs the catch, and then divides the lake’s known area by the area that the sample net covers. That ratio is the scaling factor. For example, if the lake is 1000 m² and the sample net covers 10 m², the factor is 100. The chair records that factor in the ledger along with the weight. The two other fishers verify the weight and the area calculation; if they all agree the factor stays. We keep the same factor for the rest of the week and multiply the sample weight by it to estimate the total stock. If someone doubts it, we can re‑sample or adjust the factor after a quick consensus. This keeps the estimate simple, transparent, and fair.

agent_8.question: How is proof of the required 1 kg contribution provided, and who is responsible for verifying it before the penalty is applied?
agent_8.answer:
To prove the extra 1 kg, I keep a small ledger in the communal pool area where every fisherman must sign after they deposit that extra kilogram. The deposited fish is left on the communal plank and is visible to anyone standing by. The verifier is the fisherman who is present when the deposit is made – we call them the “pool keeper” for the day. If no one is there, the next person on duty can step in and check the stack of fish; they sign a quick slip that the extra 1 kg is on the plank. If a fisher fails to deposit and the pool keeper signs a “missing 1 kg” note, a 1 kg penalty is automatically applied to their next trip unless they present the signed slip from the pool keeper showing the deposit. That way the proof is tangible (the fish itself), recorded (the ledger and slip), and verified by a community member who is present at the time.

agent_2.question: What is the community pool, what does it contain, and how is it tracked in the community’s state?
agent_2.answer: The community pool is the communal holding of fish that a fisher is forced to surrender when he or she takes more than the 0.3‑kg cap on a trip. It is kept in a shared box at the dock and is added to each time a violation is logged. The pool is recorded in the community’s shared ledger as a separate column (“Pool‑kg”) that is updated monthly. When we measure the lake stock we only count the fish that are still in the water; the fish in the pool are removed from that count. The pool can be used for communal meals, for a small income stream when we sell some fish, or as a buffer to help fishers who need a catch. Thus the pool is a tracked part of the community’s state that holds forfeited fish.

agent_5.question: How is the penalty amount calculated when the penalty is a small percentage of the excess catch?
agent_5.answer: If the penalty is a small percentage of the excess catch, we first compute how many kilograms you over‑caught beyond the allowed quota. That excess weight is then multiplied by the agreed penalty rate (the small percentage). For instance, if you exceed the limit by 2 kg and the penalty rate is 5 %, your penalty would be 0.10 kg of fish value (or the equivalent monetary amount according to the community’s conversion). In short, Penalty = Excess_Kg × Penalty_Percentage.

agent_6.question: Where is the 5kg set aside held, and who holds it until it can be returned?
agent_6.answer: We keep the 5 kg you set aside in a shared community chest at the lake’s dock, guarded by the fisher who took the catch. It’s noted in the ledger as a ‘reserve’ line item and only returned when the lake’s recorded reserve climbs back to 15 kg. Any 2 kg penalty is added to the same chest and then split among all fishers who followed the rule that round.

agent_8.question: Who is responsible for holding the communal pool and ensuring that fishers deposit the required amounts?
agent_8.answer: We all keep the communal pool in the shared container at the dock and we all deposit our excess and any required extra 1 kg before the next trip. The ledger is our shared record; each fisher writes in it. The community as a whole checks that the ledger shows the correct deposits. No single person is appointed – we rely on everyone to add what they owe and to read the ledger. If a fisher under 10 kg fails to put in the extra 1 kg, the ledger automatically records a 1 kg penalty on that fisher’s next catch, and the penalty is applied when they log their next trip.

Each fisher whose reserves are below 20 kg receives 3 kg from the pool, starting with the fisher having the lowest reserves, until the pool is exhausted. agent_9.question: Who conducts the daily biomass measurement to verify the 30% reserve, and how is the rotating village elder selected and scheduled?
agent_9.answer:
The daily biomass measurement is done by the village elder who is on rotation. Every month we hold a simple drawing of lots in front of the council, and whoever’s name is drawn becomes the elder for that month. During that month the elder is scheduled to stand at the dock at the start of each fishing day to weigh the lake’s biomass (by measuring a sample net of fish that the community catches as a ‘reference catch’ and estimating total biomass from that). The elder records the measurement on the communal ledger and signs it to confirm the 30 % reserve. If the elder is unable to perform the task (illness, travel, etc.) we call the next person in the rotating list. The rest of the community simply follows the procedure – we all record our planned catches before departure and the elder checks the total after the day.  

This procedure does not alter the proposal itself, so I restate it unchanged below. 

Policy:
"Each fisher may take no more than 1.5 kg per trip, and the community may remove no more than 30 % of the lake’s current biomass per day while always keeping at least 30 % of the biomass as a reserve."

Operationalization:
- Each fisher records intended catch on the communal ledger before each trip.
- At day’s end, total community catch is tallied.
- The rotating village elder performs the biomass measurement at the start of the day to determine the 30 % reserve.
- If any fisher exceeds 1.5 kg or the community total exceeds 30 %, the excess is forfeited and a fine of $1 per kg is imposed.
- Two consecutive days of non‑compliance triggers a one‑month suspension of fishing rights.

No changes were necessary to the policy or operationalization.

At month’s end, the council sums the logged monthly catch, checks against the 10 % cap and reserve level, and enforces forfeiture or bans as needed. If the monthly totals trigger a reserve drop below 30 % or a cap breach, fishing is suspended for 30 days and the council convenes to adjust limits if the stock has changed by more than 10 % relative or 1 kg absolute, or if a downward trend of over 5 % in three months is observed.

agent_3.question: The proposal says each fisher receives a fishing ticket for 2kg, but it does not specify who holds or distributes these tickets—does the community already have a mechanism for that or will a new one need to be established?
agent_3.answer: I will ask the community council to take on the role of ticket distribution, using the existing ledger keeper to issue tickets at the start of each month. Each fisher will receive one 2kg ticket, and the steward will record all issuances and catches in the communal ledger.

If the monthly cap is reached or the lake’s remaining stock would fall below the 1kg minimum for a fisher, ticket issuance stops and the remaining fishers may only fish to keep that 1kg. The ledger is reviewed at the end of the month to reset tickets and to decide whether fishing should pause for the following month.

agent_3.question: What criteria or mechanism does the proposal specify for deciding whether fishing should pause in the following month?
agent_3.answer: The proposal says that at the end of each month the steward looks at the ledger to see how many fish were caught and how many fish remain in the lake. If the remaining stock is less than the amount that would let every fisher keep the mandatory 1 kg for themselves (i.e., fewer fish left than the number of fishers), the steward will suspend fishing for the next month. In short, the rule pauses fishing when the lake cannot support the 1‑kg minimum for every fisher in the following month.

At month‑end the steward reviews the ledger: if the remaining stock is insufficient to allow every fisher to keep 1 kg, fishing is paused for the next month; otherwise fishing resumes under the same rules.

agent_3.question: The policy does not state what enforcement or penalty applies if a fisher fishes more than the allowed 2 kg per trip, fails to keep the required 1 kg, or otherwise violates the rule. What happens in such cases?
agent_3.answer: We don't have a formal penalty yet, but we can agree that the steward will enforce fairness by requiring return of any excess fish and revoking tickets for repeated violations. A warning will be issued first, then a ban from fishing for the rest of the month if the violation continues, and a loss of a ticket next month if it repeats.

agent_3.question: How many fishing tickets does each fisher receive at the start of each month?
agent_3.answer: One ticket per fisher, provided the lake can support that many. The number of tickets issued each month equals the number of fishers that can be accommodated while keeping at least 1 kg per fisher and respecting the 30 %/4 kg catch cap. In practice that is floor(min(0.3×LakeStock, 4 kg)÷2 kg) tickets. If there are more fishers than that, the remaining fishers receive no ticket and may only fish to keep the required 1 kg.

agent_4.question: Who is the community lead, and what authority does that role have to enforce the 8 % removal limit and administer fines?
agent_4.answer: The community lead is the fisher who is elected by a simple majority of the community at the start of each month. He or she acts as a steward, not a boss, and has the authority to tally the shared log, calculate the total removal, and enforce the 8 % limit. When a fisher exceeds 0.3 kg in a trip, the excess is returned to the lake and the lead may deduct a small fine from the fisher’s reserve, as agreed in our communal rules. The lead’s power comes from the collective agreement that we decide rules by vote and that the lead is responsible for keeping the records and applying the penalties so that we all keep the lake healthy.
agent_4.revised_policy: No fisher may take more than 0.3 kg per trip, the community may not remove more than 8 % of the lake’s current biomass in any 30‑day period, and the lake’s biomass must never fall below 4 kg; fishing is suspended until the biomass reaches 6 kg.

The lead calculates the total removal and verifies that it does not exceed 8 % of the current biomass. Monthly biomass is estimated by a rotating volunteer who counts fish. If a fisher exceeds 0.3 kg in a trip, the excess is returned to the lake and the lead fines a small amount from the fisher’s reserve. If the lake’s biomass falls below 4 kg, all fishing is halted for that month and the lake is allowed to recover to 6 kg before fishing resumes. Rules are reviewed and voted on monthly; any change requires a simple majority.

agent_4.question: Who is the rotating volunteer who counts fish, and how is their count used to estimate the lake’s biomass for enforcing the 8 % removal limit?
agent_4.answer: The volunteer is a fisher from the community who takes turns each month—usually I step in when I’m free, and otherwise a different fisherman or woman does it. We simply go to the agreed sampling point, line up the net, and count every fish that falls in. The raw number is then multiplied by the community‑agreed average weight per fish (derived from a recent market survey) to give us an estimate of the lake’s total biomass for that month. The community lead uses that estimate to calculate the 8 % removal limit: the total catch recorded by all fishers that month is divided by the estimated biomass; if the ratio exceeds 8 %, the excess is returned and a fine is imposed. This way the volunteer’s count gives us a practical, transparent estimate of how much the lake holds, allowing us to enforce the rule fairly and keep the lake healthy.

If the biomass falls below 4 kg, fishing is suspended until it recovers to 6 kg.

agent_4.question: What is the exact amount or method for determining the fine levied when a fisher exceeds the 0.3 kg per trip limit or when the 8 % removal limit is exceeded?
agent_4.answer: The fine will be calculated as a percentage of the market value of the fish that was taken in excess. For any trip that exceeds the 0.3 kg cap, the excess weight is multiplied by the agreed market price per kilogram and then 10 % of that amount is paid as a fine. For the 8 % of the lake’s biomass that is removed in a 30‑day period, the excess is multiplied by the market price per kilogram and 20 % of that amount is fined. The excess fish is returned to the community and the fine goes into the shared maintenance fund.

agent_4.question: What is a fisher’s reserve, and how is it managed and used to pay fines?
agent_4.answer: In this game the ‘reserve’ is the stock of fish a fisher keeps for his own use – the weight that he brings home each trip after the community portion is set aside. We keep the reserve in a personal net or ice chest that is part of our household. The community keeps a simple ledger (or a shared tally on the shore) that records how much each fisher has taken. When a fisher exceeds the per‑trip limit, the excess fish is returned to the communal holding, and the fine is deducted from his reserve account. If his reserve falls below the amount needed for a minimum of 1 kg per trip, he cannot fish until he rebuilds the reserve from the community maintenance fund or by trading surplus from other fishermen. Thus the reserve is both a personal safety net and a payment account for fines.

agent_5.question: Who determines the fine amount that a fisher who exceeds the monthly cap must pay?
agent_5.answer: The fine is set by the community itself – normally the rotating ledger keeper, or the small fishery council that meets each month, votes on a penalty that fits the lake’s current stock and our shared economic needs.

If a keeper is absent or declines, the following fisher on the list steps in. This keeps the role fair and transparent.

agent_5.question: How is the randomly selected community member for the monthly audit chosen, and who qualifies as a community member eligible to conduct the audit?
agent_5.answer:
We pick the auditor by a simple random draw each month. At the end of the month, the council draws a name from a bowl that contains slips for every community member on the roster except the ledger keeper for that month. The slip drawn names the auditor for the next month’s audit. Anyone who is on the alphabetical roster – that is, any active fisher or community member who has paid their dues and is not currently the ledger keeper – qualifies to be drawn. The auditor must be able to attend the audit session and has no conflict of interest with the ledger keeper. This ensures a fair, transparent, and impartial audit process. The process remains unchanged from the rest of the proposal; only the selection method and qualifications are clarified.

agent_6.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 40 kg per trip; the lake must maintain a minimum reserve of 8 kg; if the reserve falls below that, each fisher must set aside 3 kg of their catch before leaving. Before each trip, the fisher declares the intended catch on a communal ledger. The current lake reserve is checked by the community tally at the start of the trip. After the trip, the fisher deposits 3 kg into a communal reserve jar. If the fisher fails to set aside the required 3 kg, they must surrender the entire catch to the community pool. The community meets weekly to audit the ledger and, for any fisher who fails to comply twice, imposes a one‑trip fishing ban.

You can still fish up to 40 kg of fish that you intend to keep. The 3 kg you set aside is subtracted from your catch before you start fishing and is not counted against that 40 kg limit.

agent_7.question: The proposal states that excess weight is returned to the lake immediately, but it does not specify who holds the excess weight and how it is physically returned to the lake. Who is responsible for holding and returning the excess weight?
agent_7.answer: The fisher who over‑caught is the one who holds the excess weight. He/she must keep the over‑caught fish in a marked, sealed bag (or container) until the end of that trip, then deposit the bag directly into the lake at the agreed return point (the dock or a marked spot). The responsibility falls on the fisher who broke the limit – that fisher is the one who must physically return the excess fish and is barred from fishing for one week. All other fishers simply continue their normal trips.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 2 kg per trip, but the total weekly harvest cannot exceed 40% of the lake’s current stock, with a hard minimum of 4 kg remaining in the lake.
agent_7.revised_operationalization: 1. After each trip, the fisher records the exact weight of fish taken. 2. At the end of the week the community sums all catches and compares the total to the 40% cap. 3. If the total exceeds the cap, the fisher who over‑caught (the one whose trip produced the excess weight) keeps the excess in a marked, sealed bag until the end of that trip. 4. Immediately after the trip, that fisher deposits the bag into the lake at the designated return point (the dock or a marked spot). 5. The excess weight is thus returned to the lake immediately, and the fisher who over‑caught is barred from fishing for one week. 6. All data (trip weights, the total weekly catch, the excess returned, and the barred fisher) is posted publicly for verification.

agent_7.answer: I reckon the whole community should share the job of tallying the weekly catch and spotting the excess. The person who brings the fish back to the dock—often the one who keeps the ledger—will add up everyone’s trip weights, compare the total to the 40 % cap, and note any over‑catch. If someone exceeds the limit, that fisher must drop the excess back into the lake immediately and the community’s fish council will enforce the one‑week ban on that person. We’ll all post the data on the public board so everyone can see the totals and the ban applies as a community rule, not just to me.

If a fisher is barred for over‑catching, the council revokes that fisher’s permit for the next week. The revocation is recorded on the community ledger and posted next to the fishing dock so everyone can see that the fisher is ineligible until the week expires.

agent_8.question: Who holds the communal pool, and how is it administered?
agent_8.answer: The pool is kept by the community recorder in a communal chest by the pier. Every fisher records their catch and, if their reserves fall below 10 kg, contributes an extra 1 kg to that chest. The recorder tallies all deposits, holds the pool, and at month‑end distributes it to fishers whose reserves are under 15 kg, giving each no more than 2 kg. Any fisher who fails to contribute the extra 1 kg when required receives a 1 kg penalty on the next trip. The ledger tracks all contributions and penalties, ensuring transparency and fairness.

agent_8.question: How is a fisher’s reserve defined and tracked in the system, given that the current state does not include a reserve variable?
agent_8.answer: In this game a fisher’s reserve is the amount of fish weight that fisher keeps on hand after each round.  It is calculated by taking the fisher’s reserve from the end of the previous round, adding the catch from the current trip, subtracting any contribution they made to the communal pool, and then subtracting any penalty that has been applied from a previous violation.  The community recorder updates this number in the ledger every round, so each fisher’s reserve is always known to everyone before the next trip.

agent_9.question: What mechanism is used to detect and enforce the 1.5 kg per trip limit, and how is each fisher’s catch weight recorded?
agent_9.answer: We detect the 1.5 kg per trip limit by making each fisher weigh his haul at the dock (or in the boat with a portable scale) right after he pulls his line.  He records the weight on a catch card and hands the card to the community leader. The catch weight is then recorded in the ledger in the community hall with the fisher’s name, the trip number, the weight, and the date/time, so the daily tally of removals is transparent and can be checked against the 30 % limit.  This system makes it easy to see who has exceeded the limit and to enforce the rule immediately, while the reserve check by the monitor ensures the lake never falls below 30 %.

agent_9.question: If the daily removal tally shows that the community would exceed the 30% lake‑biomass limit, how does the community leader enforce that limit?
agent_9.answer:
If the daily removal tally shows we’re headed for more than 30 % of the lake’s biomass, the leader must stop fishing that day before any new trips.  The leader reviews the ledger each morning; if the cumulative planned catch (including any catch that has already been weighed but not yet released) would push us over the 30 % ceiling, he says "no one may depart for the rest of the day" and announces the suspension to all.  If a fisher has already departed and the ledger shows that adding his catch would exceed the limit, the leader calls the fisher back to the dock, forces him to return the excess portion of his haul to the lake, and, if the fisher refuses or if the over‑limit persists, the leader suspends that fisher’s right to fish for the rest of the day (or for a specified number of days).  This enforcement is done by the leader physically preventing boats from launching, by requiring catch to be placed back in the lake, and by recording the suspension in the ledger so the community can see the penalty.

•  Pool Management: After each trip, any catch beyond 2 kg is placed into the communal crate.  The keeper logs the total pool amount each month.  On the first day of the next month the keeper opens the crate, counts the kilos, and distributes the pool equally among all fishers whose reserves are below 15 kg, giving each a maximum of 2 kg (or the remaining pool if less).  The distribution is recorded in the ledger.
•  Penalty Enforcement: If a fisher fails to contribute the mandatory 1 kg when below 12 kg, the keeper records the violation and, on the next trip, seizes exactly 1 kg of that fisher’s catch and places it directly into the communal pool.  If the fisher’s catch is less than 1 kg, the entire catch is treated as the penalty.  The penalty is noted in the ledger and cannot be reclaimed.

agent_1.question: What does the 2% cumulative limit refer to, and over what period is it calculated?
agent_1.answer: The 2 % cumulative limit means that any single fisher’s total catch over the last twelve months may not exceed two percent of the lake’s current biomass. In other words, you keep a rolling tally of all the fish you’ve taken in the past year; that tally must stay below 0.02 × ( current lake biomass). If you exceed that amount you must return the excess to the communal reserve and pay a penalty equal to its market value. The period of calculation is a twelve‑month sliding window that resets as each month passes, so your yearly catch is always measured against the latest lake biomass.

agent_3.answer: When the lake’s stock drops below 8 kg the rotating ledger‑keeper, who already keeps the monthly totals, is responsible for recomputing the proportional cap. At the very start of the next month the keeper calculates the new cap (40 % of the new stock, capped at the lower of 6 kg or the scaled amount) and posts the figure on the communal notice board and in the ledger so every fisher knows the limit. Each trip the fisher records the take; if a trip exceeds the current cap the keeper immediately records the excess and returns it to the pool (by putting the fish back or by charging a fee). Because all takes are logged in real time, the pool balance is always visible and the cap is automatically enforced by the ledger system.

agent_4.answer: The council will impose the fine. After the weekly log is submitted, the council tallies each fisher’s monthly catch. If a fisher has exceeded 3 kg, the excess amount is multiplied by a set rate – say 2 lira per kg of excess – and that sum is deducted from the fisher’s share of the community fund. The fine goes into the replenishment pot that pays for planting aquatic vegetation and other conservation work. This keeps the penalty directly tied to the fish that were taken in excess and gives the community a clear incentive to stay below the cap.

agent_4.question: What is the process for measuring the lake’s biomass to determine when it reaches 5 kg and fishing may resume?
agent_4.answer:
We must know how much life the lake still holds before we let our nets touch it again. Every month, on a calm morning, the council will take a small gill‑net out of the water at a handful of random spots around the lake. The net sits for two hours, then we haul it in, count every fish and weigh the whole catch. From that sample we calculate the average weight per fish and the density of fish per square metre. Multiplying that average by the estimated number of fish in the whole lake gives us a rough estimate of the lake’s total biomass. If that estimate falls below five kilograms, the council will announce that fishing may resume, but only under the limits in the policy. Until that threshold is met, we keep the nets closed and help plant more aquatic vegetation so the fish can grow again.

The measurement is done each month, and the result is recorded in the council’s log. The same monthly log of each fisher’s catch is also kept. Both are checked together to enforce the 12 % removal cap and the 3‑kg monthly cap. When any fisher exceeds the 3‑kg cap, the excess is returned and a fine of 2 lira per kg of excess is paid into the replenishment fund.

So, in short: monthly sample nets → weigh & count → extrapolate biomass → if <5 kg → fishing restarts under the rules; if >12 % of current biomass is taken that month, the whole community is barred for that month; if the lake ever drops below 3 kg, fishing is suspended until it rises to 5 kg, and extra replenishment actions are taken.

agent_5.question: How is each fisher’s share of the 70% monthly limit determined and allocated among the fishers?
agent_5.answer: The 70 % monthly limit is a community‑wide ceiling – it’s the total amount that all of us together can pull out in a month. After the steward records the lake’s stock at the start of the month, we calculate 70 % of that figure. That 70 % is then split evenly among the fishers who actually go out that month. If a fisher’s catch pushes the community total over the 70 % limit, he is considered in violation and must reduce his next month’s catch by 10 % of the lake’s current stock and/or give half of his next month’s catch to the pot. agent_6.question: Who verifies that a fisher has set aside the required 1 kg when the lake reserve falls below 3 kg?

After each trip the fisher will record the exact catch on a shared ledger and, if the reserve drops below 3 kg, will set aside the 1 kg immediately. The next fisher on the lake, or a randomly chosen community observer, will then check the ledger and the physical 1 kg to confirm it’s been set aside. If the fisher fails to do so, the observer will note it, and the fisher will forfeit the entire catch next round and pay the fee. This way everyone has a clear, low‑cost method of verification without needing a dedicated official.

The rule itself stays the same; only the verification process is clarified.

The next fisher on the lake or a randomly chosen community observer will verify that the 1 kg has been set aside by checking the ledger and the physical fish. If a fisher fails to set aside the required 1 kg, they forfeit their entire catch for the next round and must pay a small fee to the community fund.

agent_6.question: How is a random community observer selected, and what are the qualifications for serving as an observer?
agent_6.answer:
To pick an observer, we use a simple method. Every time a fisher takes a trip, we ask the next fisher who will come to the lake after them. If there is no next fisher scheduled yet, we choose someone from the community present at the dock using a fair roll of a six‑sided die; the number shows the position in a list of all community members who signed up for observer duty that week. The observer must be a person who has no stake in the catch of the current fisher, must have a clean record of past observations, and must be able to count fish accurately. They should also have the respect of their neighbors and be willing to report honestly.

We keep a short list of approved observers on the community board. Each observer signs a small pledge that they will be impartial and will not take any of the fish in the locked chest.

So, the selection is random when the next fisher is not already chosen, and the qualifications are honesty, impartiality, a clean record, and basic fish‑counting skill.

agent_7.question: What exactly is a fisher's 'weekly allowance' that can be forfeited for a violation, and how is that allowance calculated?
agent_7.answer: Your weekly allowance is simply the amount you are allowed to take in a single week under the 70 % cap.  Each week the keeper weighs the lake, multiplies the weight by 0.70, and that number is the total amount the whole community may harvest that week.  An individual fisher’s allowance is the portion of that total that he has already taken; if you add another trip and the sum of all fishers’ catches would exceed the 70 % cap, you must return the excess.  If you ever take more than 2 kg in one trip or drive the community’s weekly total over the cap, you forfeit your next week’s allowance and must give your catch to the communal reserve.  In short: the weekly allowance is the 70 % of the lake’s stock that is legally harvestable for the week, and it is calculated by the keeper at the start of each week.

If the cumulative weekly catch would exceed the cap, the last fisher to exceed must return the surplus to the lake or to the communal pot.  Anyone who violates the trip or weekly limits will forfeit his next week’s allowance and must donate his catch to a communal reserve for future shortages.

agent_7.answer: The keeper is the fisher elected by the community each week, usually the one who has shown most respect for the rules. He can require the offending fisher to immediately return the surplus to the lake or the communal pot, and he can enforce the penalty that the fisher forfeits his allowance for the next week and must donate his catch to the communal reserve. The keeper also holds the right to refuse any future trips to anyone who has violated the limits until the penalty has been paid, ensuring the rules are respected.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify who holds the communal pool of fish and how it is distributed among fishers each month.
agent_8.answer:
The pool isn’t a secret stash; we’ll keep it in the community boat shed, in a lockable crate that the fish‑keeper—say the one who always watches the dock—tends. After every trip we log the catch and, if the total of the crate is ready for the month, the keeper opens it, counts the kilos, and on the first day of the next month hands out the fish. We’ll make a simple ledger: each fisher’s name, their monthly reserve before the trip, the 1‑kg contribution if they were below 12 kg, the 2‑kg keep limit, and the extra that landed in the crate. At month’s end we look at the ledger, find everyone whose reserve is under 15 kg, split the crate’s total equally among them, and cap it at 2 kg each. That’s how the pool is held and distributed. I’ll stick to the wording of the rule; only the logistics of holding and giving it out were missing.

The community will rotate the keeper so no one person is overloaded, and we’ll keep the ledger in the shed so everyone can see it whenever they like.

Fisher with reserves below 12 kg must contribute an extra 1 kg per trip to the pool; failure to do so results in a 1 kg penalty on the next trip. The pool is redistributed monthly to fishers whose reserves fall below 15 kg, capped at 2 kg per fisher per month.

At the end of each month, the keeper counts the total fish in the crate. The total is divided equally among those whose reserves are under 15 kg, with each fisher receiving a maximum of 2 kg. Anyone who did not contribute the mandatory 1 kg when below 12 kg receives a 1 kg penalty on their next trip’s catch.

agent_8.question: How is the keeper chosen and how is the rotation schedule determined for tending the communal pool?

All fishers who have kept at least 1 kg on their last trip and who have contributed the mandatory 1 kg when their reserve was below 12 kg are eligible to vote. Fishers who missed a contribution or are currently under penalty are not eligible for that month. The fisherman who receives the most votes becomes the keeper for the next month. If there is a tie, the keeper is selected by drawing lots from the tied candidates. The keeper serves for one month, tending the lockable crate, recording the catch, and handing the crate over to the next keeper when the month ends. This rotation keeps the job fair and ensures that the person in charge has proven reliability.

agent_8.answer:

Then, as soon as the fisher pulls in the net, the keeper seizes exactly 1 kg of fish—no more, no less—from the haul before the catch is split. That 1 kg is moved straight into the communal pool. If the fisher’s catch turns out to be less than 1 kg (for example, they only managed 0.8 kg), the entire catch is treated as the penalty and is deposited into the pool, leaving the fisher with nothing from that trip. The keeper updates the fisher’s record, and the penalty is considered served once the 1 kg is deposited. No other deductions are made; the fisher’s reserve can’t dip below zero because the penalty is a removal of fish, not a subtraction from the reserve balance.

The authority comes from the community’s agreement in the rules; if the steward misbehaves the community can vote to replace them.

The steward collects this fine directly from the fisher’s ledger entry on the day of the catch, usually within a few days.  The fine is strictly monetary; the fish itself is returned to the lake and no extra fish is taken.

agent_1.question: What is the mechanism for enforcing the penalty of forfeiting catch and losing fishing rights for one month when a fisher exceeds the limits?

If someone’s logged total for the month exceeds the 2 % monthly limit or the per‑trip limit, the Watcher marks the excess and informs the community. The fishers then vote by simple majority: a fisher who over‑catches must return the surplus to the communal reserve and is barred from fishing for the next calendar month. agent_4.question: When and how exactly is the lake’s biomass measured to determine whether it is below 6 kg and to calculate the 8 % removal limit each month?
agent_4.answer: We measure the lake’s biomass first thing on the 1st of each month. A council member and a few fishers will do a quick visual census or a standard net‑haul estimate, and the result is written into the shared logbook. That number is the biomass that the whole month refers to. If the figure is below 6 kg, the council declares a fishing halt and no one may fish until the next monthly survey shows 6 kg or more. The 8 % removal limit for the month is calculated as 8 % of that same 1st‑of‑month biomass. All catches are logged each day, and at the end of the month the council tallies the total removal and compares it to the 8 % threshold; if it’s exceeded, the excess must be returned and the fisher does one day of community labor.

agent_5.question: Who holds the responsibility for recording the lake's stock at the start of each month?
agent_5.answer: It’s the community’s job, handled by the community leader or the appointed recorder. We don’t do the counting ourselves, we just trust that the leader writes the stock at the start of each month.
agent_5.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 30% of the lake’s current stock per trip, capped at 8 kg, and may not cumulatively take more than 70% of the lake’s stock at the start of each calendar month. At the start of each month, the community records the lake’s stock. No fisher may take more than 70% of that amount across all trips that month. On each trip, the fisher records the weight taken; if the sum of that fisher’s catches that month would exceed the 70% limit, the fisher must stop fishing that month. If a fisher exceeds the 30% or 8 kg per trip limit, the community records a violation and the fisher loses fishing rights for that day and must pay a small fee or perform community service. Violations are checked weekly by the community leader. If the lake falls below 10 kg, all fishing stops until it recovers to 20 kg to ensure recovery.

If a fisher violates on multiple trips in a month, the fees are summed. This way the penalty scales with the amount of over‑catch and makes the cost proportional to the harm caused.

agent_7.answer: As a fisher I reckon the counting of the lake stock and the announcement of the weekly harvest cap belong to the community’s elected lake monitor. Every week a fisher is chosen—by rotation or a quick vote—to step forward, physically gauge the lake’s current stock using our standard measuring device, and then announce the 60 % cap to everyone before the trip. This way the task is shared, transparent and cannot be abused by a single person.

If the lake is below 2 kg when the week begins, we switch the weekly cap to 30 % and the per‑trip limit to 1 kg for that week.  The monitor announces the cap at the first meeting before the first trip, and the same cap applies to every subsequent trip that week.

agent_7.question: How is compliance with the per‑trip limit and cumulative weekly cap verified and enforced, and who is responsible for holding and updating the communal ledger that records these catches?
agent_7.answer:
We’ll keep the lake monitor as the eye that sees the numbers. Before you head out, each of us signs a simple “intent” sheet that says how many kilos we plan to haul. The monitor checks that sheet and makes sure it’s no more than 1.5 kg per trip and that the total of everyone’s intents for the week stays under the 60 % cap (or 30 % if the stock is under 2 kg). After the trip you report the actual catch; the monitor tallies it against your intent. If you over‑step the per‑trip limit or the week’s cap, you must return the extra kilos and you’re slapped with a one‑week fishing ban. All the numbers go into the communal ledger that the lake monitor keeps on a ledger board in the fish house and copies are sent to the community council each week.

A fisher’s monthly allowance is therefore the sum of all of their legal trips that do not exceed the community cap.  If a fisher records a catch that exceeds the 1.5 kg per‑trip limit, fails to keep the required 0.5 kg, or pushes the community total over C, the recorder rejects that trip and requires the fisher to return the excess.  The recorder then reduces that fisher’s allowance for the following month by the amount of the over‑take, so they are given less total fish that month to compensate for the breach.

agent_3.answer: The recorder does the reduction. After a fisher is found to have taken more than allowed, the recorder subtracts the over‑take from that fisher’s previous monthly allowance. The new allowance is never lower than the minimum that lets the fisher keep at least 0.5 kg per trip. The recorder writes the new monthly allowance in the shared ledger so the fisher knows the limit for the next month.

The ledger is signed only if all checks pass.

agent_3.question: What is each fisher's initial monthly allowance at the start of a month, and how is that allowance determined and recorded in the ledger?
agent_3.answer: At the start of every month the recorder takes the lake’s measured stock S and computes the communal cap C = min(0.30 × S, 3 kg).  The recorder then assigns each fisher an equal share of that cap – the initial monthly allowance A for every fisher is A = C ÷ N, where N is the total number of fishers who have signed the ledger.  This allowance is written into the shared ledger as a line item for each fisher.  During the month, each trip is logged with the amount taken and the portion kept. If a fisher is found over the limit, the recorder reduces that fisher’s allowance by the over‑take (but not below the minimum that still allows a 0.5 kg keep per trip) and records the new allowance for the next month.  The ledger is signed only when all checks have passed.

agent_4.answer: In the rules we agreed, the community volunteer who weighs each haul will also be in charge of collecting any fines and notifying the council about suspensions. The council, once notified, will enforce the one‑month suspension by revoking the fisher’s permit for that period.

So if a fisher is caught on June 12, the one‑month suspension covers July 1–July 31. agent_5.question: Which mechanism will enforce the requirement to return excess catch and impose a one-day fishing ban when a fisher exceeds the 30% per trip or 60% monthly limits?
agent_5.answer: We use the community ledger as the enforcement tool. Each fisher writes down the weight of the fish taken immediately after the trip. The group meets daily to reconcile the ledger against the lake’s current stock. If a fisher’s log shows a catch that exceeds the 30% trip limit or the 60% monthly limit, the other fishers will insist that the excess be returned to the lake and that the fisher sit out the next fishing day. This peer‑monitoring, backed by a collective agreement, keeps the rule in place without a formal authority. If disputes arise, a designated fishing steward can step in to mediate.
agent_5.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 30% of the lake’s current stock per trip, capped at 4 kg, and may not cumulatively take more than 60% of the lake’s stock at the start of each calendar month. At the start of each month the community records the lake’s stock. Each fisher logs their catch on a shared ledger and may not take more than 30% of the stock present at the start of their trip or exceed 4 kg per outing. Once a fisher’s total monthly catch reaches 60% of that month’s initial stock, they must wait until the next month. If someone exceeds limits, the community requires them to return the excess to the lake and sit out one fishing day. The rule is reviewed quarterly; if the lake’s stock consistently stays above 5 kg, the 60% limit may be increased.

Thus the ledger gives a clear, audited record of the lake’s stock at the start of the month and the cumulative catches each fisher has taken, allowing us to enforce the limits.

If the committee cannot reach a majority, the council chair (the person who chairs the monthly meeting) will make the final decision. This keeps the process transparent and locally accountable.

agent_6.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the committee will verify that a fisher has left the required 5 kg in the lake after a trip – what evidence or verification process is used?
agent_6.answer:
We’ll make the verification a simple, community‑based check. Every fisher will note the lake’s weight on a shared log before they leave and take a photo of the lake after they finish fishing, with the timestamp and a witness (anyone who saw them leave the 5 kg in the lake) signing the log. The committee will review the photo and the witness signature. If the photo shows the lake’s weight is still at or above 5 kg and the witness confirms the fisher left the 5 kg, we trust the record. If the photo or witness can’t be provided or the lake’s weight is below 5 kg, the committee will investigate – maybe do a quick spot check the next day or ask for a re‑take of the photo. This keeps the process low‑tech, community‑driven, and hard to cheat. I’ve kept the core numbers the same; only added the photo‑and‑witness step for verification.

agent_7.question: Who composes the council of representatives, how many members are there, and how are they selected?
agent_7.answer: The council is made up of one representative from each active fisher each week. There are usually ten members—one per fisher—and they are selected by a quick vote among the fishers. The top ten catchers for the week are the ones who sit on the council, and each week a new member is elected by majority vote to keep the representation fair.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may take no more than 1.5 kg per trip, and the community’s weekly total harvest may not exceed 50% of the lake’s current stock, with a hard minimum of 2 kg remaining. If the lake falls below 4 kg, the weekly harvest limit halves.
agent_7.revised_operationalization: After each trip, each fisher records catch on the shared log reviewed weekly by the council of representatives. The council calculates the lake’s current stock and applies the 50% rule; if the total exceeds the limit, the violating fisher pays a fine equal to 10% of the overage and is barred from fishing the next week. If the lake stock drops below 4 kg, the council halves the weekly harvest limit to 25% and lowers the per‑trip limit to 0.75 kg. Failure to record catch or to comply with the limits results in a temporary loss of fishing rights until the next cycle.

agent_7.question: When does the council recalculate the lake’s current stock and apply the 50% rule and the 4‑kg threshold—at the start of the week, after each trip, or at the end of the week—so it’s clear which stock level is used for determining limits and penalties?
agent_7.answer: We only recalc the lake’s stock once each week – right before the first trip of that week – using the stock measured at the end of the previous week. That figure sets the 50 % limit and the 2 kg minimum for the whole week. If, at any point during the week, the stock falls below 4 kg, the council immediately recalculates the limits for the remainder of the week: the weekly harvest cap is cut in half (to 25 % of the new stock) and the per‑trip limit drops to 0.75 kg. Fines and bans are imposed at the end of the week after the council tallies all catches for that week.

agent_7.question: If a fisher fails to record a catch, how is the fine of 10 % of the overage determined and who is held responsible for the payment?
agent_7.answer:
If a fisher never puts his catch on the log, the council treats the missing amount as the catch that he would have been allowed to take. The weekly cap is still the 50 % of the lake stock (or 25 % if the lake fell below 4 kg). The council looks at the sum of all recorded catches. The difference between the cap and that sum is the overage attributable to the unrecorded fisher. That overage is 10 % of the fine that the fisher must pay, and the fine is collected from the fisher himself. If the unrecorded catch would actually exceed the per‑trip limit, the council simply treats it as the maximum the fisher was entitled to take; the fine is still 10 % of the excess over the cap. In short, the fisher who forgets to record is personally liable for the fine and the ban.

agent_7.question: How is the ban from fishing the next week enforced and verified by the council or community?
agent_7.answer:
To make the ban work we keep it in plain sight and in the hands of everyone. Each morning the council writes the names of any fishers banned for the next week on the community board and reads them aloud at the dawn gathering. Every banned fisher must hand over a piece of his gear—usually a small hook or a net tag—as collateral. If a banned person shows up at the dock, the council refuses him any boat or gear and tells him to come back next week. The gear is held until the ban expires or until he pays any fine. We also keep a ledger of all recorded catches and check it every week; if an unrecorded trip turns up in the ledger we flag the fisher, issue the fine, and automatically add his name to the ban list for the following week. The combination of public notice, collateral, and ledger checks keeps the ban enforceable and verifiable. The community can’t cheat because anyone can see who is banned and why, and the council has a concrete record of each case.

If a fisher tries to fish while banned, the council confiscates the gear and can even issue a further fine for the violation. The ban is only lifted when the week is over and the fisher pays any outstanding fine or returns the collateral.

The system works because it’s simple, visible, and tied directly to the ledger we already use for catch records. No one can hide a ban, and everyone knows the rules and consequences.

agent_8.question: Which existing mechanism will hold the communal pool and track each fisher’s reserve?
agent_8.answer: We already keep a shared ledger right by the dock – the community keeper writes down each trip’s catch, the pool balance and everyone’s reserve. That ledger is our pool and reserve tracker; the keeper updates it after every catch and each month’s distribution, so we all know what the pool holds and what each fisher’s reserve is.

agent_8.question: How is the lake’s stock monitored and updated, and how does that affect the rule that all fishers pause when the lake falls below 5 kg until the pool replenishes?
agent_8.answer: I keep a tally of the fish I catch each trip. After I pull the net I count the weight, subtract it from the lake’s current stock that the community keeps on a shared ledger. If the lake is at 5 kg or more I can keep up to 3 kg and put any excess in the communal pool. When the ledger shows the stock has fallen below 5 kg, we all stop fishing – none of us can pull the net until enough fish from the pool (or from the lake’s natural replenishment) bring the stock back up to 5 kg. That’s why the pause rule is tied to the lake’s stock: it protects the lake from being over‑fished when it’s already low.

agent_8.question: How is the lake’s stock restored to 5 kg when it falls below that threshold—does the community move fish from the communal pool back into the lake stock, and if so, who authorizes and records that transfer?
agent_8.answer:
The lake’s stock is brought back up to 5 kg by moving fish from the communal pool back into the lake.  That transfer isn’t automatic – it has to be agreed on by the fishers.  When the stock dips below 5 kg we all pause, then hold a quick vote among the active fishers.  A simple majority authorises the transfer.  The designated ledger keeper then records the movement: the pool is reduced by the amount moved, and the lake stock is increased to 5 kg.  That way everyone can see exactly how many kilos were put back, and no one can secretly take fish from the pool to the lake.
