All fishers consult the ledger before each trip; if a fisher’s name shows an active ban, the steward will refuse to register the catch and may also remind the fisher that the ban is in effect. The ban is automatically lifted when the end date is reached; the steward marks the entry as “lifted” and the fisher may resume fishing. Only the steward, acting as the community’s verifier, has the authority to lift a ban—once the prescribed period has elapsed and no new violations have occurred. If a fisher attempts to fish while still banned, the steward can extend the ban and the fisher must remain off the lake until the new end date.
agent_2.revised_policy:
When the lake’s stock is above 5 kg, each fisher may harvest up to 1 kg per trip; when the stock is 5 kg or less, each fisher may harvest no more than 0.3 kg per trip. In all cases the community’s total monthly harvest may not exceed 10% of the current lake stock and at least 25% of the stock must remain as reserve. If the lake’s stock falls below 4 kg, fishing is suspended for 30 days.

If any fisher takes more than 0.3 kg per trip, that excess catch is forfeited and the fisher receives a 15‑day ban. At the month’s end, the total catch is compared to the 10% cap; if exceeded, the excess is returned and violators receive a 30‑day ban. Monthly stock assessments ensure the reserve stays ≥25%; if it falls below, fishing is halted until the reserve rises.

10. If there is a significant discrepancy in the stock record, fishing is suspended until a new, verified count is obtained.

If the number is higher, the excess is noted as forfeited, and the steward enters a 15‑day ban in the ledger. To guard against tampering, a second fisher will randomly verify a handful of catches by weighing the same haul on a separate scale and recording it in a duplicate ledger. Any discrepancies beyond five percent trigger a review and potential temporary suspension until a new count is agreed upon. This way, every individual catch is visible, traceable, and subject to the same rules that protect our lake.

agent_4.question: When and how is the lake’s biomass measured and recorded to trigger the 5% removal limit and the automatic suspension when it falls below 4 kg?
agent_4.answer: The lake’s biomass is measured once each 30‑day cycle, on the last day of the month, by a community‑appointed surveyor. The surveyor conducts a standardized catch‑per‑unit‑effort net haul (or, if available, an acoustic survey) to estimate the total biomass of the lake. The value obtained is recorded in the shared ledger as the ‘starting biomass’ for the next cycle. All catch logged in that cycle is subtracted from this starting figure to calculate total removal. If the cumulative removal for the cycle exceeds 5 % of the starting biomass, the surplus amount is returned to the lake and the community collects a small fee to fund maintenance. Whenever a measurement is taken and the recorded biomass falls below 4 kg, the rule triggers an automatic suspension of all fishing activities; fishing remains suspended until the next measurement shows the biomass has risen to 6 kg, at which point normal activity resumes. This schedule keeps measurement practical, aligns with the 30‑day removal limit, and ensures that the suspension threshold is enforced promptly.

The community as a whole may remove no more than 5 % of the lake’s current biomass each 30‑day period. If the lake’s biomass falls below 4 kg, fishing is suspended until it reaches 6 kg. All catch is logged in a shared ledger and reviewed by a community‑appointed surveyor who measures the lake’s biomass on the last day of each month and records the result in the ledger.

If removal > 5 % of starting biomass, the surplus is returned to the lake and a fee is recorded. • Suspension trigger: If the recorded biomass at any measurement falls below 4 kg, a flag is set in the ledger, all fishing activity is halted automatically, and a notification is sent to the community. Fishing resumes only after the next measurement shows the biomass has reached 6 kg. All operations are transparent and auditable in the shared ledger.

agent_4.question: How are the 0.3 kg per trip and 1 kg per fisher per month limits enforced, and what happens if a fisher logs a catch that exceeds those limits?
agent_4.answer:
In our ledger we already keep a running tally of each fisher’s trips and the weight they log. The system checks two thresholds: the per‑trip cap of 0.3 kg and the monthly cap of 1 kg. When you record a trip, the ledger compares the value to 0.3 kg. If you exceed it, the ledger flags the line as an over‑capture and locks it until you resolve the issue. The same goes for the monthly total – the ledger keeps a running sum of your catches each month and will flag if the sum ever goes beyond 1 kg.

When a flag is raised, the next step is to correct the over‑capture. You must return the excess to the lake within three days, and you must inform the surveyor. The surveyor will measure the lake again and record the return in the ledger. The ledger will then apply a small fee (e.g., 0.1 kg worth of fish) that goes into a community buffer pool for future restocking. If you fail to return the excess or to pay the fee within a week, the surveyor can issue a suspension notice: your fishing rights for the next 30‑day cycle will be halted until the ledger shows compliance. agent_6.answer: We’ll put a simple system in place: every trip a fisher will log their catch and the lake’s remaining weight in a shared ledger that the community can see. At the end of each round the lake‑keeper or a rotating community watcher will review the ledger entries. If a fisher’s record shows that the lake fell below 4 kg and they did not set aside the required 2 kg, the keeper will issue a penalty. The penalty is to skip the next fishing trip; a second offense will require the fisher to give their entire next catch to the lake’s reserve. This way everyone knows who checks, what the rule is, and how the consequence is applied without needing a formal court or fines.

Any excess fish are added to a communal pool that is redistributed monthly to fishers whose reserves are below 12 kg, capped at 2 kg per fisher per month. Fishers whose reserves are below 8 kg must contribute 1 kg per trip to the pool; failure to do so results in a 1 kg penalty on the next trip.

At the end of each month, the pool is divided equally among all fishers with reserves under 12 kg, giving each up to 2 kg. If a fisher failed to contribute the required 1 kg, the following trip’s catch is reduced by 1 kg as a penalty.

agent_8.question: How does the community record that a fisher has a pending 1 kg penalty and enforce the subtraction of 1 kg from their next trip’s catch?
agent_8.answer:
We keep a simple, visible ledger on the dock. When a fisher who is under 8 kg skips his 1 kg contribution, the next fisherman who finishes the trip will see a note next to the fisher’s name: “Penalty: 1 kg pending.” That note stays on the ledger until the fisherman takes his next trip. On that trip he first reads the ledger, sees the 1 kg penalty, subtracts that kilogram from the total he actually catches, and then applies the normal 3 kg keep‑limit. If his raw catch was 4 kg, he subtracts the 1 kg penalty, leaving 3 kg, so nothing goes into the pool. If his raw catch was 5 kg, after the penalty he has 4 kg, keeps 3 kg, and 1 kg goes to the pool. The ledger then marks the penalty as satisfied and removes the note. Everyone knows that the penalty is a temporary subtraction, not a new catch, so it’s easy to enforce.

We keep this simple because we’re a small community that can’t afford bureaucracy. The ledger is checked by the next fisherman who finishes, and the penalty is applied immediately when the fisher reads the ledger. That’s how we make sure nobody gets away with skipping the 1 kg contribution.

agent_4.question: What defines a "trip" in this proposal?
agent_4.answer: A "trip" is any continuous fishing outing that starts when I leave shore (or the dock) and ends when I return to shore or dock. It counts each departure; if I go back to shore and later set out again, that is a separate trip.
agent_4.revised_policy: Fishing is suspended until the lake’s biomass reaches 6 kg; thereafter each fisher may take at most 0.25 kg per trip, no more than 3 trips per month, and the community as a whole may not remove more than 5 % of the current biomass in any 30‑day period. agent_5.question: If a fisher exceeds the 70% cumulative limit, how exactly is his next trip catch reduced proportionally?
agent_5.answer:
If you end up with a cumulative catch of, say, 80 % of the lake’s stock at the start of the month, that 80 % is 1.142… times the 70 % limit. For the next trip I’d take the same amount I was originally allowed to take that day (or the limit that day, whichever is smaller) and multiply it by the ratio 70 % ÷ 80 % ≈ 0.875. In other words, every kilogram you were planning to haul in is multiplied by 0.875, so your catch is cut to about 87.5 % of what you would normally bring in. The same scaling is applied for any other percentage that exceeds the 70 % threshold.
